web_content_rtb__content.value:
The Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus aligns with the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus to provide opportunities for integrated delivery.

Through collaborative curriculum planning, it may be decided that Life Skills outcomes and content are the most appropriate option for some students with intellectual disability.

Organisation of Legal Studies 11–12

The Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus is structured around key legal concepts and structures, the meaning and purpose of justice, and the legal issues that affect individuals, groups and society. In Year 11, students investigate the key processes of Australia’s legal system, from its creation to the current system. In Year 12, students examine the foundations of the domestic and international legal systems, the core principles underpinning the criminal justice system and Australia’s relationships with other countries. Through the selection of options, students learn about specialist fields in the law, including consumer, family, housing, workplace, and peace, conflict and the law.

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Legal Studies 11–12.

Image long description: The 4 focus areas for Year 11 are Investigating the law, Disputes under the law, Changing the law and Experiences with the law. The 2 core focus areas for Year 12 are The criminal justice system and International relations and human rights. The 5 options for Year 12 are Consumer law, Family law, Housing law, Peace, conflict and the law, and Workplace law. Legal themes and Legal skills sit in the middle of the diagram, each surrounded by a box.

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
The Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus enables students to develop knowledge and understanding of the domestic and international legal systems and how they have been shaped over time. Students investigate the key features of the law and understand how the law interacts with aspects of society.

What students learn

Through the study of Legal Studies 11–12, students:

  • develop an understanding of the foundations of law, the criminal justice system, and international relations and human rights
  • explore the role of the law in society and how laws are made and changed
  • develop an understanding of how the law operates in practice
  • develop skills in analysis and reasoning to make judgements about the extent to which the law achieves justice for individuals, groups and society
  • construct reasoned arguments supported by a range of evidence.

Course structure and requirements

Year 11 course structure and requirements

The Year 11 Legal Studies course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 4 focus areas.

Students are required to study all 4 focus areas of the course.

Year 11 focus areasIndicative hours
Investigating the law40
Disputes under the law25
Changing the law25
Experiences with the law30

Changing the law

In this focus area, students examine TWO case studies of law reform:

  • the recognition of land rights in NSW and native title for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • ONE other case study of law reform selected from NSW or the federal level.

Both case studies will draw on the following elements in the process of law reform in NSW and Australia:

  • reasons for change
  • drivers of change
  • processes of change
  • outcomes of change.

Case studies must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any content to be attempted in the Year 12 Legal Studies course.

Experiences with the law

In this focus area, students examine TWO case studies of groups that have experience with the law:

  • young people
  • ONE other group must be selected from:
    • Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
    • asylum seekers, refugees or migrants
    • LGBTQIA+ people
    • older people
    • people experiencing climate injustice
    • people experiencing economic disadvantage
    • people experiencing issues of equity, discrimination or power imbalance
    • people living in rural, regional or remote Australia
    • people who are culturally and linguistically diverse
    • people with disability
    • people with a mental health condition.

Both case studies must examine:

  • the nature of the group’s experience with the law
  • ways to access justice
  • the responsiveness of the law.

Case studies must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any content to be attempted in the Year 12 Legal Studies course.

Year 12 course structure and requirements

The Year 12 Legal Studies course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 3 focus areas
  • TWO options.
Year 12 focus areasIndicative hours
The criminal justice system (core)30
International relations and human rights (core)30
Options60

Options

Students must study TWO options from:

  • Consumer law
  • Family law
  • Housing law
  • Peace, conflict and the law
  • Workplace law.

Legal themes and skills

The Legal themes and skills offer insight into the nature of the legal system and allow students to engage in the analysis and judgement of the effectiveness of the law in achieving justice. The Legal themes and skills are to be integrated throughout the course.

Case studies and the use of evidence

The Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus embeds the use of case studies throughout course content. The use of a case study allows students to deepen their understanding of legal concepts and apply their knowledge to different situations.

A case study refers to a real-world example that illustrates a course concept, a specific legal matter, a court decision or the use of legislation. Case studies offer opportunities for students to examine the application and impact of the law. They can be used to explore, compare and contextualise legal concepts. The syllabus specifies in which areas case studies are to be used.

Across Years 11 and 12, the selection of case studies must include a range of examples that are:

  • recent and significant
  • from Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander experiences
  • a mixture of Australian and international.

The Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus requires students to incorporate a wide range of evidence to inform their understanding and support their judgements. This evidence includes legislation, cases, media, international instruments, documents, expert opinions and statistics.

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Law and the Community Life Skills offers opportunities for students to learn about the roles, rights and responsibilities of individuals and groups in the context of law in our society. Students develop skills to interact with their community and navigate the law, including making informed decisions and accessing information and support.

What students learn

Through the study of Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12, students:

  • explore the roles, rights and responsibilities of individuals and groups in communities and the importance of rules and laws in maintaining safety and fairness
  • explore how and why rules and laws change, and how they can participate in their community and have a voice in decisions that affect them
  • explore ways to access appropriate information and support related to the law
  • develop skills to communicate, seek help when needed and build relationships to participate confidently in their communities.

Course structure

Law and the Community Life Skills Year 11 and Year 12

The following focus areas can be studied throughout Year 11 (120 hours) and Year 12 (120 hours).

  • Investigating the law
  • Disputes under the law
  • Changing the law
  • Experiences with the law
  • The criminal justice system
  • Human rights
  • Consumer law
  • Family law
  • Housing law
  • Peace, conflict and the law
  • Workplace law

For Law and the Community Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The outcomes describe the knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of teaching and learning. Teachers should use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content included in each focus area.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 outcomes and content, and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • Where appropriate, students should have the opportunity to develop knowledge and understanding of key themes and skills related to law and the community. Relevant themes and skills should be integrated throughout the course based on the strengths and needs of individual students.
  • Real-world applications of the law, such as from the media, case studies and student experience, should be used where appropriate to provide opportunities for students to develop their understanding and demonstrate achievement of the outcomes.
  • Examples provided in the content are suggestions only. Teachers may use the examples provided or use other examples to meet the particular needs of individual students.

Law and the Community themes and skills

The Law and the Community themes and skills offer insight into the nature of the legal system and allow students to develop knowledge and understanding of how the legal system connects with different parts of the community. The themes and skills are to be integrated throughout the course.

Case studies and the use of evidence

The Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus provides opportunities to use case studies throughout the course content. Case studies can be used to deepen students’ understanding of how the law works. The case studies help students connect legal ideas to actual situations and learn how the law affects people, communities and society. They give students the opportunity to think critically, ask questions and explore the legal system in action.

A case study refers to a real-world example that illustrates court decisions, legal changes, laws that impact specific groups, or human rights issues. Case studies can be studied in the following focus areas.

  • Changing the law: students may undertake a case study to explore ONE rule or law that has changed in the community OR a rule or law that should be changed.
  • Experiences with the law: students may undertake a case study to explore how ONE or more groups in the community experience the law and the ways in which justice is achieved. Groups may be selected from the list below.
    • Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
    • Asylum seekers, refugees and migrants
    • LGBTQIA+ people
    • Older people
    • People experiencing climate injustice
    • People experiencing economic disadvantage
    • People experiencing issues of equity, discrimination or power imbalance
    • People living in rural, regional or remote Australia
    • People who are culturally and linguistically diverse
    • People with disability
    • People with a mental health condition
    • Young people
  • Human rights: students may undertake a case study to explore ONE human rights issue affecting individuals or groups in Australia.

The selection of case studies should include a range of examples that are:

  • recent and significant
  • from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander experiences
  • a mixture of Australian and international.

In the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus, evidence from a range of sources can be used to support students' understanding and judgements about the law.

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Understanding the roles, rights and responsibilities of individuals and groups helps students engage in their communities and recognise the importance of rules and laws in maintaining fairness and safety. By learning about the rule of law and how laws are made in Australia, students can better protect their rights, participate in the community and develop independence. Exploring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore and international legal frameworks fosters Cultural awareness and broadens students’ understanding of legal principles in various contexts.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘the role of laws in the community’, the outcome requires that a student ‘describes the purpose and application of laws for specific contexts’.

To do this, the teacher could provide students with a scenario where neighbours are consistently playing loud music late at night. Students learn about noise restrictions and identify if the neighbours in this scenario are breaking these restrictions. Verbally, in writing or by selecting words or phrases, students communicate reasons for having noise restrictions and suggest ways these might be enforced.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Development of law as a reflection of society’s values – when learning that laws in this country are made by the Parliament of Australia, students learn that the law to mandate the wearing of seat belts was introduced in 1971 to increase safety when driving or riding in a vehicle.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, students might develop evaluation skills by explaining the effectiveness of a law using criteria such as:

  • Accessibility: is the law easy to understand and use?
  • Availability of resources: are there enough people or is there enough money to apply the law correctly?

Considerations

  • Build on students’ prior learning about Federation and the Australian Constitution in the Life Skills focus area Australia: Making a nation – from Federation to WWI from the History 7–10 Syllabus when teaching about laws and parliament.
  • Introduce the concept of laws by connecting this with students’ understanding of rules in familiar contexts (e.g. home and school).
  • Demonstrate ways that students can access appropriate information or support related to their rights (e.g. refer to the websites of advocacy groups, community groups, legal services or Government agencies).
  • Provide opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning using their preferred communication form(s). This could include a presentation outlining the process of creating a new law or using digital tools to develop a poster to illustrate a class rule.
  • Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may benefit from access to linguistic supports when learning vocabulary related to parliament, courts and laws.
  • Provide opportunities for students to engage with the local Aboriginal Community to learn about Cultural Knowledges, including the significance of Customary Lore for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.

Connecting with Legal Studies 11–12

Teachers may program Law and the Community Life Skills content by integrating it with content from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with outcomes from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

Below is an example of how the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus

Legal institutions

  • The role, jurisdiction and hierarchy of courts in New South Wales and Australia
The teacher provides the names and roles of courts and a diagram that shows the court hierarchy in NSW and Australia.

Students are given a legal scenario to determine and explain which court(s) would have jurisdiction to hear the case.

The teacher provides students with a list of each court and an example of a case each court deals with. They provide a supporting diagram that shows the court hierarchy in Australia.

Students consider a scenario based on a legal case and identify which court would deal with the case.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area explores Australia’s legal framework and how it has evolved.

Students develop an understanding of the legal system in Australia and how our system of law has developed. Using a range of examples, students examine the meaning of law and its aim to protect individuals and regulate society. Using current media reports, case studies or hypothetical scenarios, teachers can demonstrate how the legal system operates in practice, both in Australia and internationally.

When examining legal foundations, students explore key concepts such as justice and the law and the role of regulating the actions of individuals. Teachers can illustrate this by exploring a range of issues that demonstrate differing perspectives of individuals and groups.

Students will explore the rich history of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore, and compare it with the development of the Australian legal framework, including common law, statute law and the Constitution. Teachers should illustrate the structure and function of the law, the intention is not for students to focus on the history of the law. Students examine the impact of international law and how it has influenced our legal system. Teachers may illustrate this by selecting a global issue for study, students should have the opportunity to observe the ways in which the United Nations and other organisations shape participation in international law and regulate relationships between nations.

Making connections

Teachers should begin this focus area by establishing students’ prior knowledge of the law and the legal system. Prior knowledge may include laws that apply specifically to children and young people, such as compulsory attendance at school.

Teachers should select relevant real-world examples to support students understanding of how the legal system functions in their daily routines, whether they are shopping online, catching a bus to school or navigating the process of applying for part-time work.

This focus area may be taught concurrently with the focus area Experiences with the law and the case study on Young people. Teachers could make connections to the ways in which young people experience the law, including connections with common law, statute law and international law. When choosing a second case study to examine, teachers may select content points that link specifically to that group. For example, if the group is ‘people with disability’, the teacher might link to the content point ‘domestic and international protection of rights’.

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

Ensure students’ wellbeing and safety when designing and delivering teaching and learning for Legal Studies 11–12 by adhering to relevant legislation, regulations and standards that enable a safe and supportive learning environment for students.

Key skills

  • Define key legal terminology.
  • Research and analyse media reports to highlight key concepts.
  • Classify laws according to their type and source.
  • Examine a range of contemporary issues or problems to reflect the difficulties in the law.
  • Read and analyse legal cases that feature key syllabus concepts.

The use of evidence

In Legal Studies, students develop their understanding of the law through investigating and analysing a range of evidence from a variety of sources. Evidence can be used to demonstrate how the law operates, support or refute an interpretation of the law, or inform legal reasoning.

Teachers can support students to effectively use evidence by:

  • selecting cases that highlight the function of the law and/or the difficulties in achieving justice
  • emphasising the distinction between legislation in different jurisdictions, for example NSW or Australia
  • using media reports, case studies or hypothetical scenarios that demonstrate how the legal system operates in Australia and internationally
  • using media reports to illustrate situations where justice may or may not have been achieved.

Key terminology

  • access
  • adversarial system
  • common law
  • Constitution
  • Customary Lore
  • division of powers
  • doctrine of precedent
  • domestic law
  • equality
  • ethics
  • fairness
  • hierarchy
  • intergovernmental
  • international law
  • jurisdiction
  • justice
  • law
  • legislation
  • nation-state
  • non-government organisation
  • procedural fairness
  • referendum
  • responsibilities
  • rights
  • rule of law
  • separation of powers
  • state sovereignty
  • statute law

Vocabulary development is essential to support learning in Legal Studies and is best taught in context. Explicit teaching of key terms will assist students to develop knowledge and skills.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Understanding how and why rules and laws can change helps students recognise that they can have a voice in decisions that affect them. Learning about changing the law enables students to explore fairness, build confidence in expressing their ideas and develop respectful ways to ask for change. Through learning about ways to advocate for legal change, students develop skills in communication, decision-making and advocacy, preparing them to take part in life at school, work and in the broader community.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘ways to advocate for changes to rules in different contexts’, the outcome requires that a student ‘examines ways that laws are made and changed’.

To do this, the teacher could present a scenario where students campaign to change a school rule. Students inquire into who the rule affects, why a change is requested and how students can respectfully raise their views. Using words, images or symbols, students sequence the steps involved in proposing and implementing the change.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Development of law as a reflection of society’s values – when learning about why rules and laws change, students explore how community needs and values influence decisions. For example, changes to school uniform policies may reflect growing awareness of cultural inclusion, gender expression or climate considerations.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when teaching about the reasons that laws change, students have the opportunity to develop skills in interpretation by considering questions including:

  • Why was this rule or law introduced?
  • Does it meet the needs of everyone in the community?
  • What might happen if the rule or law does not change?

Case studies

In this focus area, students may explore a case study to support their understanding of changing the law.

The case study may be of a rule or law that has changed, or a rule or law that students think should change. For example, changes to:

  • rules about the use of mobile phones in school
  • sporting association rules
  • laws related to the use of social media
  • Australian marriage laws.

Considerations

  • Introduce the concept of changing the law by connecting with students’ experiences of rule changes in familiar settings, including school, home or work.
  • Explore how changes to rules or laws come about, such as through feedback from students or families, meetings with leadership, or community consultation.
  • Break down the steps in the change process using visuals, such as timelines, flowcharts or sequencing templates.
  • Provide opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning using their preferred communication form(s). This could include writing a persuasive text or delivering an argument orally, digitally or using assistive technology to communicate their ideas about a rule they think should be changed.
  • Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may benefit from opportunities for oral interaction and use of home language(s) or dialect(s) in collaboration with peers to practise and develop vocabulary and communication skills.

Connecting with Legal Studies 11–12

Teachers may program Law and the Community Life Skills content by integrating it with content from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with outcomes from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

Below is an example of how the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus

Reasons for change

  • Addressing the needs of individuals, groups or society
The teacher introduces a change to the law that responded to a specific need in society, such as flexible working arrangements.

Students describe the issue, explain how the need was identified and outline the steps or process taken to address it.

Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus

Reasons for change

  • Reasons rules change in communities to which individuals and groups belong
The teacher introduces a change to the law that responded to a specific community need, such as flexible working arrangements.

Students identify who was affected, sequence what happened and communicate why the change was important, using visuals, short text or supported oral responses.

Purpose

Understanding consumer law helps students make informed decisions when buying goods and services. Students learn about their rights as consumers, their responsibilities and what to do if something goes wrong. They explore common contracts, such as mobile phone plans or online subscriptions, and learn how to respond to unfair practices or faulty products. By exploring ways to respond to consumer law issues, students develop confidence and skills to seek help and take appropriate action if their consumer rights are breached.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘types of consumer contracts’, the outcome requires that a student ‘identifies rules and laws for individuals and groups’.

To do this, the teacher could introduce examples of consumer contracts, such as gym memberships, phone contracts or online subscriptions. Students identify the terms and conditions they will be agreeing to and what their responsibilities are by using words or gestures. Students may practise checking for terms and conditions using digital or printed materials or asking questions before signing up.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures in achieving justice for individuals, groups and society – when learning about ways to respond to a breach of contract, students explore the role of fair-trading bodies or consumer tribunals and how these measures resolve disputes and protect consumers.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when teaching about credit services, students can develop skills of interpretation by recognising and asking questions about the terms and conditions of a loan or credit card.

Students might also develop investigation and research skills by exploring how to find relevant information before making a purchase. This may include identifying where to find reliable reviews or using evidence from more than one source to determine if a price is competitive.

Considerations

  • Introduce the concept of a consumer using real-life experiences, such as buying goods or services from retail stores or online providers.
  • Build on students’ existing knowledge and skills about online safety by explicitly teaching about ways to identify or avoid consumer scams.
  • Demonstrate ways students can respond to problems with a purchase, such as returning a faulty item or contacting a help service.
  • Provide opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning using their preferred communication form(s). This could include creating a checklist for safe online shopping or presenting a scenario showing how to interact with retail staff when returning a product.
  • Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may benefit from access to linguistic supports, including multilingual websites, when learning about consumer law.

Connecting with Legal Studies 11–12

Teachers may program Law and the Community Life Skills content by integrating it with content from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with outcomes from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

Below is an example of how the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus

The nature of consumer law

  • Contracts as a key function of consumer protection against unfair business practices
The teacher explains the elements of a legally binding contract using hypothetical scenarios (or real case law examples).

Students analyse how consumer contracts are used to protect rights and identify the risks if the terms are unclear or unfair.

Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus

Consumer rights, responsibilities and law

  • Consumer contract terms and conditions
The teacher presents an example of a familiar consumer contract and identifies key features, such as cooling-off periods or payment requirements.

Students use this as a model to identify features in other examples of contracts, and to identify key aspects of the contracts that consumers should check before signing an agreement.

Purpose

By exploring common types of disputes, such as those involving agreements or contracts, students develop their understanding of when and how to seek help, along with skills in communication and decision-making. This learning supports students to understand their rights and responsibilities, build respectful relationships and participate more confidently and independently in their communities.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘legal agreements or contracts in everyday contexts’, the outcome requires that a student ‘describes the purpose and application of laws for specific contexts’.

To do this, the teacher could introduce annotated or adapted examples of contracts for familiar situations, such as a streaming service. Students describe the purpose and key terms of these contracts and identify what can happen if terms are not followed by matching actions (e.g. ‘not paying my bill’) with consequences (e.g. ‘streaming service is suspended’).

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Relationship between law, justice and society – when learning about how disputes are resolved, students explore how laws and legal processes help individuals and groups live safely and fairly in the community.
  • Effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures in achieving justice for individuals, groups and society – when exploring ways to resolve conflict, students consider the role of the legal system alongside other methods like mediation.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when teaching about legal agreements or contracts in everyday contexts, such as rental agreements or mobile phone plans, students can develop interpretation skills by exploring relevant laws and how they affect people. This may include considering questions such as:

  • What are the relevant laws and what is their purpose?
  • Who is affected and how?

Considerations

  • If students have completed Commerce in Years 7–10, build on prior learning from the Life Skills content group Resolving disputes in the Commerce 7–10 Syllabus.
  • Present dispute resolution as a continuum, showing both informal and formal options including peer mediation, support from adults, police involvement and courts.
  • Explicitly teach strategies for conflict resolution and provide opportunities for students to practise conflict resolution skills using strategies such as scripts, modelling and scenarios.
  • Provide opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning using their preferred communication form(s). This could include students creating a storyboard or using assistive technology to demonstrate how they would resolve an issue.

Teachers may program Law and the Community Life Skills content by integrating it with content from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with outcomes from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus

Civil law

  • Procedures in NSW tribunals and civil courts, including alternative methods of resolving disputes
The teacher outlines a range of methods commonly used for resolving conflict between individuals and groups. They present a range of scenarios about disputes in different contexts, such as neighbourhood disagreements or workplace issues. Students analyse and respond to these disputes.

Students determine and explain the most appropriate method to reach resolution in each scenario.

Resolving disputes

The teacher introduces ways to resolve disputes using familiar examples. They present a range of scenarios about disputes in different contexts, such as arguments between friends, neighbourhood disagreements or workplace issues. Students analyse and respond to these disputes.

Purpose

Understanding that people can have different experiences with the law helps students recognise their rights and responsibilities. Students explore how factors such as age, ability or background can influence the way individuals interact with legal systems. Students learn how to respond safely, identify legal support and develop their understanding of the importance of fairness and respectful communication.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘reasons why groups need protection under the law’, the outcome requires that a student ‘investigates the relationship between the law, justice and the community’.

To do this, the teacher could provide students with a scenario where a young person is bullied and harassed online. Students recognise the need to protect young people in online environments and consider relevant laws and how they can be used to address this issue.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Relationship between law, justice and society – when exploring how vulnerable groups may experience the law differently, students consider whether the law is applied fairly and justly across all groups in society.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when undertaking a case study of a group and their experiences with the law, students can develop skills in analysis and use of sources by considering whether information from firsthand accounts is fact or opinion.

Case studies

In this focus area, students may conduct a case study of how one or more groups in the community experience the law and the ways in which justice is achieved. The case study may focus on how a legal situation affected a person or group, including how their experience was influenced by factors such as age, culture, ability or location.

Sources of information about how groups in the community experience the law and achieve justice could include:

  • firsthand accounts
  • data from surveys or focus groups
  • media reports, documentaries or podcasts
  • statistics or information from official sources, including government reports.

Considerations

  • Provide opportunities for students to make choices related to case studies, such as selecting the group(s) to be studied, focus questions for the research, methods of research, materials they engage with or the ways they communicate their learning.
  • Ensure students recognise the strengths of groups, not just their vulnerabilities. For example, recognise that young people have strengths, such as the ability to readily adopt new technologies to find information and support when experiencing legal challenges.
  • Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may benefit from access to linguistic supports and the use of home language(s) or dialect(s) when generating ideas and planning for case studies.
  • Explicitly teach students how to identify and connect with people, groups or organisations that could provide support if they experience issues with the law.

Connecting with Legal Studies 11–12

Teachers may program Law and the Community Life Skills content by integrating it with content from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with outcomes from the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus.

Below is an example of how the Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Legal Studies 11–12 Syllabus

Responsiveness of the legal system

  • Barriers to achieving justice
The teacher provides students with examples of barriers that may affect young people seeking justice, such as language, cost, lack of legal knowledge or discrimination.

Students analyse how these barriers may affect young people using a range of sources and explore how the legal system addresses or fails to address these issues.

Law and the Community Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus

Case study

  • Issues of equity and justice experienced by the group
The teacher provides students with examples of barriers that may affect the case study group when seeking justice, such as language, cost, lack of legal knowledge or discrimination.

Students identify how these barriers could affect the group’s experience with the law.

Purpose

Understanding family law helps students to recognise the rights and responsibilities of individuals in families and how the law can support people during times of change, conflict or harm. Learning about ways to access information and support in family contexts assists students to develop help-seeking skills and strategies.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘measures to protect vulnerable individuals in families’, the outcome requires that a student ‘identifies legal information and support’.

To do this, the teacher could introduce information about relevant laws and sources of support, including police liaison officers, government departments or safety planning services. Students identify trusted adults, organisations or services they could contact if they or someone they know needed help.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Relationship between law, justice and society – when learning about the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children to maintain a connection with their Culture, students explore how laws and care arrangements support children to stay connected to family, Community, Language and traditions. Students consider how legal protections reflect community values and promote justice through cultural continuity.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when teaching about the role of courts in resolving family disputes, students can develop investigation and research skills by engaging with a range of sources, such as websites or narratives, and using scaffolded secondary research to answer questions about how courts can be used to provide resolutions in family disputes.

Considerations

Understanding housing law helps students recognise their rights and responsibilities when looking for or living in a home. Understanding human rights helps students recognise freedoms and protections and their sense of responsibility towards upholding the rights of themselves and others. The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘human rights that apply to all individuals’, the outcome requires that a student ‘identifies rights or responsibilities of individuals and groups in the community’.

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, when teaching about international human rights, students can develop skills of analysis and use of sources by exploring materials such as posters, websites or news stories about global human rights and considering whether the source is factual and whose perspectives it includes.

Purpose

Understanding the roles, rights and responsibilities of individuals and groups helps students engage in their communities and recognise the importance of rules and laws in maintaining fairness and safety. By learning about the rule of law and how laws are made in Australia, students can better protect their rights, participate in the community and develop independence. Exploring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore and international legal frameworks fosters Cultural awareness and broadens students’ understanding of legal principles in various contexts.

Planning for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

The outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. Teachers use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content points.

For example, when teaching the syllabus content, ‘the role of laws in the community’, the outcome requires that a student ‘describes the purpose and application of laws for specific contexts’.

To do this, the teacher could provide students with a scenario where neighbours are consistently playing loud music late at night. Students learn about noise restrictions and identify if the neighbours in this scenario are breaking these restrictions. Verbally, in writing or by selecting words or phrases, students communicate reasons for having noise restrictions and suggest ways these might be enforced.

Themes

Law and the Community themes can be integrated throughout the focus area to provide a context for learning.

For example:

  • Development of law as a reflection of society’s values – when learning that laws in this country are made by the Parliament of Australia, students learn that the law to mandate the wearing of seat belts was introduced in 1971 to increase safety when driving or riding in a vehicle.

Skills

Opportunities to develop the Law and the Community skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example, students might develop evaluation skills by explaining the effectiveness of a law using criteria such as:

For example, when teaching about global conflict, students can develop skills in analysis and use of sources by exploring news reports, images or case studies about peacebuilding efforts and examining the different ideas presented.

This focus area examines how law reform acts as a tool to reflect changing values and update the law.

Students develop an understanding of the need for, and operation and implications of changes to the law through the lens of 2 case studies of law reform. Students explore the reasons for change, such as the need for relevance, the demand for justice and social considerations. They also explore the drivers, processes and outcomes of change.

Through an investigation of the process of law reform, students examine case studies in NSW or Australia which demonstrate how law reform may be influenced by factors such as international forces, the adoption of a new law, the simplification of the law or defects in an existing law. Teachers should use examples from a variety of sources that illustrate the causes and challenges involved in changing the law or establishing a need for change.

By examining the purpose of law reform through the case studies, students consider the unintended consequences of change and the effects on the integrity of the legal system. Examples of these consequences and effects may include: the attrition of the rights and freedoms of others, impacts on resource allocation or cost, judicial interpretations that may not be in the spirit of the amendment (e.g. loopholes), or the difficulty of enforceability.

In the first case study, students explore the recognition of land rights in NSW and the framework provided for Aboriginal land claims before investigating native title. This case study focuses on the significance of individual initiatives, policy reviews and changing social values that have led to recognition. Teachers should highlight the implications of developing native title laws through common and statute law and consider areas of compensation, future treaties, parliamentary representation and the importance of cultural preservation to understand the motivation behind this area of law reform.

Making connections

Teachers should establish prior knowledge of law reform and the need for change to develop important connections for students. Using recent changes to the law that apply to young people or an international event, students could explore and identify reasons why the law has changed and who or what has driven these changes. Students draw on the role of common law and statute law to inform their understanding.

This focus area establishes important links to the content in Year 12 including the need for law reform in The criminal justice system (core) and the International relations and human rights (core) focus areas, as well as the options. 

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

Ensure students’ wellbeing and safety when designing and delivering teaching and learning for Legal Studies 11–12 by adhering to relevant legislation, regulations and standards that enable a safe and supportive learning environment for students.

Key skills

  • Define key legal terminology.
  • Explain the relationship between law reform and the reasons for change.
  • Critically analyse the implications of law reform for individuals, groups and society.
  • Evaluate the implications of changes to the law from a variety of perspectives.
  • Demonstrate awareness of advocacy by becoming active citizens in relation to law reform.

The use of evidence

In Legal Studies, students develop their understanding of the law through investigating and analysing a range of evidence from a variety of sources. Evidence can be used to demonstrate how the law operates, support or refute an interpretation of the law, or inform legal reasoning.

Teachers can support students to effectively use evidence by:

  • selecting case studies that highlight the process of law reform
  • emphasising the distinction between law reform in different jurisdictions, for example NSW or Australia
  • using media reports, case studies or expert opinions that demonstrate how the need for reform is established.

The use of case studies

Teachers should consider the needs and interests of students when selecting a second case study. The following areas of reform could be considered:

  • animal rights
  • copyright
  • cyberbullying
  • data privacy
  • defamation
  • discrimination
  • driving
  • environmental protection
  • Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP)
  • innovations posing concerns for the law, such as AI or other new technology
  • juvenile detention
  • policing
  • protection of rights and freedoms
  • relationships
  • social media.

When exploring a driver of change, students should consider both informal and formal drivers of change in NSW and at a federal level. Informal drivers could include advocacy groups, non-government organisations and trade unions. Formal drivers could include the following:

NSWFederal
NSW Law Reform CommissionAustralian Law Reform Commission (ALRC)
State parliamentary committees and inquiriesFederal parliamentary committees and inquiries
NSW OmbudsmanCommonwealth Ombudsman
NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC)Royal commissions
NSW Office of the Children’s GuardianAustralian Human Rights Commission (AHRC)

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area examines how disputes are resolved under the law.

Students explore the purpose and characteristics of criminal law, civil law and administrative law and distinguish between them. They examine each area of law through the lens of a relevant case or dispute that reflects the operation of the law, its procedures and outcomes. Legal personnel could include magistrates, judges, solicitors, barristers, the Director of Public Prosecutions, Public Defenders and police prosecutors. When examining the outcomes of a criminal or civil case, teachers may explore the relevance of the verdict, the punishments or the remedies handed down. Teachers should select a case with a final decision as this will enable a more thorough application of key syllabus concepts and court procedures.

Students develop an understanding of the importance of individual rights for suspects and the accused in criminal law due to the power and resource imbalance between the individual and the state. When investigating civil law, students examine the ways in which disputes are resolved through a combination of methods, often beginning with alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and, if that fails, going to court as a last resort. Teachers should explore a mediation process and a tribunal established to resolve disputes relating to consumer law, tenancy, discrimination, employment or family.

In examining disputes with the state, students develop an understanding of the reasons the state enacts legislation to pursue outcomes that protect society. Teachers may address the ways in which state actions impact individual rights and freedoms resulting in disputes with the state, such as state regulation that impacts freedom of speech, freedom of association or freedom of movement. Students consider the effectiveness of measures used when individuals and/or groups are in dispute with the state. This should include the influence of non-legal measures on the outcome of a dispute, including involvement from non-government organisations, advocacy groups and the media.

When considering each area of the law, students must examine the purpose, outcomes and the way in which the law resolves disputes through a real-world example. For each case or dispute, teachers should consider:

  • how the case or dispute reflects social values
  • how the law in relation to the case or dispute is enforced
  • how the state’s actions achieve their intended outcome
  • the extent to which rights and freedoms are impacted (positively and negatively)
  • how the outcomes of the case illustrate principles such as the rule of law and procedural fairness
  • opportunities to undertake appeal and review.

Court visit

Teachers may consider opportunities for students to observe the operation of a court or tribunal through a court visit (in person, virtually or by watching a documentary) to support student understanding in this focus area. Teachers should carefully select court experiences reflective of needs and backgrounds of students. Adjustments may be needed to enable student participation in court visits.

Making connections

Teachers should begin teaching and learning in this focus area by relating concepts such as statute law and common law from the focus area Investigating the law with the intended purpose of law. For example, one intended purpose of the law is to provide a framework to resolve disputes between individuals.

When students examine the process of resolving disputes under criminal law, important links can be formed to the criminal justice system as addressed in the Year 12 core. Opportunities exist to make connections with ways to resolve disputes through courts and tribunals, which is later addressed in the Year 12 focus area International relations and human rights, and the Year 12 options.

This focus area may be taught concurrently with the focus area Experiences with the law. For example, while examining Case study 1: Young people, students may explore the way in which young people seek justice for a dispute with a government organisation.

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

Ensure students’ wellbeing and safety when designing and delivering teaching and learning for Legal Studies 11–12 by adhering to relevant legislation, regulations and standards that enable a safe and supportive learning environment for students.

Key skills

  • Define key legal terminology.
  • Distinguish between criminal and civil law procedures.
  • Explain the rights of individuals in criminal and civil disputes, and in disputes with the state.
  • Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of alternative methods of resolving disputes.
  • Apply criteria to evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures.
  • Use hypothetical scenarios to examine different perspectives of justice for individuals, groups and society.

The use of evidence

In Legal Studies, students develop their understanding of the law through investigating and analysing a range of evidence from a variety of sources. Evidence can be used to demonstrate how the law operates, support or refute an interpretation of the law, or inform legal reasoning.

Teachers can support students to effectively use evidence by:

  • referring to cases from state and federal levels that illustrate the procedures and methods used to resolve disputes
  • providing opportunities to synthesise and integrate a range of legal information to assist understanding
  • using a range of media reports to highlight areas of effectiveness in resolving disputes that can lead to valid and well-reasoned judgements
  • analysing a range of expert opinions and reports to help build foundational knowledge and understanding
  • providing a scaffold to support the comparison of 2 sources about the same dispute, such as a High Court summary and a news article.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area explores Australia’s legal framework and how it has evolved.

Students develop an understanding of the legal system in Australia and how our system of law has developed. Using a range of examples, students examine the meaning of law and its aim to protect individuals and regulate society. Using current media reports, case studies or hypothetical scenarios, teachers can demonstrate how the legal system operates in practice, both in Australia and internationally.

When examining legal foundations, students explore key concepts such as justice and the law and the role of regulating the actions of individuals. Teachers can illustrate this by exploring a range of issues that demonstrate differing perspectives of individuals and groups.

Students will explore the rich history of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore, and compare it with the development of the Australian legal framework, including common law, statute law and the Constitution. Teachers should illustrate the structure and function of the law, the intention is not for students to focus on the history of the law. Students examine the impact of international law and how it has influenced our legal system. Teachers may illustrate this by selecting a global issue for study, students should have the opportunity to observe the ways in which the United Nations and other organisations shape participation in international law and regulate relationships between nations.

Making connections

Teachers should begin this focus area by establishing students’ prior knowledge of the law and the legal system. Prior knowledge may include laws that apply specifically to children and young people, such as compulsory attendance at school.

Teachers should select relevant real-world examples to support students understanding of how the legal system functions in their daily routines, whether they are shopping online, catching a bus to school or navigating the process of applying for part-time work.

This focus area may be taught concurrently with the focus area Experiences with the law and the case study on Young people. Teachers could make connections to the ways in which young people experience the law, including connections with common law, statute law and international law. When choosing a second case study to examine, teachers may select content points that link specifically to that group. For example, if the group is ‘people with disability’, the teacher might link to the content point ‘domestic and international protection of rights’.

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

The use of evidence

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area develops an understanding of the interrelationship of the law across national boundaries and the standards set in place to protect human rights across the globe.

Students develop a broad understanding of the interconnection of global affairs and human rights protection. Through examining the collaboration of nation-states and the interactions between international actors, including intergovernmental and non-government organisations (NGOs), students explore strategies used to protect individuals and avoid conflict. Students assess the effectiveness of international law in safeguarding human rights, with a focus on the role of legal and non-legal measures.

When teaching content outlined under the content group headings, teachers should consider the following advice.

The nature of international relations

Teachers may begin with an introduction to International relations, through which students gain a deeper understanding of how state sovereignty influences the pursuit of human rights globally. Students may investigate the provisions in the UN Charter on state sovereignty to discover how this principle underpins effective international cooperation. They may explore why protecting state sovereignty is essential for a unified global approach to human rights. By examining the impact of international organisations, students may gain an understanding of the vital role of international relations in recognising and advancing human rights for all.

The nature of human rights

Teachers may begin by examining the characteristics of human rights to develop an understanding for students of how international instruments provide a framework for their protection. Students explore the types of rights included in treaties and conventions and how they have changed over time. They should be given the opportunity to investigate the impact of change and the emerging areas of human rights protection, such as digital rights and climate justice.

International protection of human rights

Teachers should introduce the key functions of the United Nations, alongside other organisations, courts and tribunals and how they protect human rights and respond to breaches. Students examine the ways in which human rights breaches are reported and investigated through the role of organisations such as the Human Rights Council and the Special Rapporteur. Relevant courts may include the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice; and relevant tribunals could include the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Tribunal for Yugoslavia (ICTY).

Australian protection of human rights

Teachers may begin by examining the dualist approach that Australia uses to incorporate international human rights instruments into Australian domestic law. Students examine the process of signing and ratifying treaties and conventions, and the need for the enactment of domestic legislation for them to become legally binding. Students should investigate the diverse roles of the Australian Human Rights Commission through a recent inquiry or submission.

Promotion of human rights

Teachers may begin with an exploration of how the promotion of human rights differs from the protection of human rights. Students investigate the importance of raising awareness of human rights at international and domestic levels. They examine a range of NGOs and media that raise awareness of breaches and that pressure nations to improve the standard of their human rights protection. Students should look to recent examples of how international organisations have improved the standards of human rights within nations.

Making connections

Teachers may build on knowledge from the Year 11 content group The global legal system in the focus area Investigating the law, in which students were introduced to international customary laws, the United Nations, courts and tribunals. Students should go beyond the framework of international law to form a critical understanding of how institutions function under the influence of nation-states.

Content from the Year 11 focus area Disputes under the law will assist students to develop conceptual thinking on individual rights and freedoms and the needs of the state. Through examples of the implementation of human rights under international instruments, students will develop their understanding of the content from Changing the law at an international context.

Links to the criminal justice system and the options are provided by exploring individual human rights and the need to protect them. Similarly, a grasp of the role of advocacy, NGOs and the media will assist students to understand ways of supporting individuals, groups and society.

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

Ensure students’ wellbeing and safety when designing and delivering teaching and learning for Legal Studies 11–12 by adhering to relevant legislation, regulations and standards that enable a safe and supportive learning environment for students.

Key skills

  • Analyse cases at a domestic and international level that feature human rights concepts.
  • Explain the relationship between key human rights concepts and the achievement of justice.
  • Critically analyse the limitations of international law and the degree of protection of human rights.

The use of evidence

In Legal Studies, students develop their understanding of the law through investigating and analysing a range of evidence from a variety of sources. Evidence can be used to demonstrate how the law operates, support or refute an interpretation of the law, or inform legal reasoning.

Teachers can support students to effectively use evidence by:

  • selecting examples that highlight the functions and limitations of human rights law implementation
  • considering the reliability and bias of sources by distinguishing between expressions of political rhetoric and legally protected rights
  • analysing case studies that demonstrate the domestic and international protection of human rights
  • investigating examples that show how international law impacts both the global community and Australia’s local context.

Accessing information on a range of organisations provides an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding. Information from the following organisations may be helpful for accessing legal practice when teaching this focus area.

Suggested organisationsApplication of learning
The United Nations (UN)Investigate the powers of the UN Charter and the actions of the UN to maintain peace and security.
The International Criminal Court (ICC)Examine the role of the court and the reason why it acts as a court of last resort.
The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC)Explore the ways human rights are promoted and investigate a recent project.
Australians for Native Title and Reconciliation (ANTAR)Explore the role and initiatives of an NGO.

The use of case studies

When considering a case study, students investigate the extent to which a human right is protected at an international level or in Australia. This is best explored through ways a human right is protected and enforced by law or by investigating ways in which a human right has been breached. Case studies can be examined either as standalone content points or integrated into the teaching of other content in this focus area. Students could research a human right such as the right to:

  • be free from slavery, breached through human trafficking or forced labour
  • life, breached using capital punishment
  • freedom of expression, including freedom of speech, breached through censorship and restrictions on access to information
  • liberty, breached through arbitrary detention
  • self-determination, the recognition and protection of traditional lands for Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • education, breached through the use of child soldiers in armed conflict
  • a clean, healthy and safe environment, protected through domestic legislation
  • freedom of movement, protected through international law
  • freedom of religion in Australia, protected through a combination of constitutional provisions, anti-discrimination legislation and international law
  • a fair trial, including the presumption of innocence, protected through common-law principles and international law.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area explores how the criminal justice system works to balance the rights of victims, offenders and society through its processes and institutions.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to develop knowledge and understanding of the NSW criminal justice system. Using a range of evidence, students analyse current issues from a range of perspectives, including those that impact defendants and offenders, victims and society. Students examine the processes within the criminal justice system, from the investigation by police to pre-trial measures, the criminal trial, sentencing and post-sentencing. In analysing these processes, students should consider issues of balance between individual rights and the needs of the community, access to the law and the extent to which justice is achieved.

When teaching content outlined under the content group headings, teachers should consider the following advice.

The nature of crime

Teachers should consolidate understanding of the definition and elements of crime and highlight for students the reasons why individuals commit crimes, which could include self-interest, economic gain, addiction, mental health and social influences. When exploring situational and social crime prevention strategies such as the installation of physical barriers to restrict access or promoting community involvement in safety initiatives students should consult recent initiatives.

Investigation

Teachers may begin by referencing key legislation that regulates police powers and the use of discretion to consider individual circumstances and make judgements based on specific situations in investigating crimes. Teachers may give students the opportunity to examine the range of powers that enable police to enforce the law and maintain order, while also considering how individual rights and the needs of society need to be balanced against these powers. By exploring support measures for the victim and the accused, students are provided with an opportunity to investigate the importance of fairness and transparency in the investigation process.

Pre-trial

Teachers may begin by exploring the need for pre-trial processes to balance society’s need for efficiency and safety while upholding individual rights before a trial. This could include a discussion of court attendance notices and case conferencing, including charge resolution and early guilty pleas (or equivalents as these processes evolve). Students may examine the reasons why bail may be granted or refused and the type and number of conditions set, rather than an overly heavy emphasis on reforms.

Trial

Through an introduction to court hierarchy, students may examine the intentions of the adversarial system and its merits when it comes to achieving procedural fairness. Students may consider areas where a less adversarial approach might better protect the rights of victims and witnesses, such as restorative justice processes. Students may also examine the relationship between society’s changing values and the development of the law, through reforms like the use of juries or judge alone trials.

Sentencing

Teachers may begin by examining the steps involved when an accused pleads guilty or is found guilty in a court of law that leads to sentencing. Matters such as the impact of crime on victims and society may be explored. Students investigate how judicial discretion in sentencing is necessary for decisions which reflect the circumstances of the offending and the offender, as well as ensuring consistency over time. The consideration of alternative approaches to sentencing offers students an opportunity to explore options for vulnerable offenders and Culturally appropriate sentencing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, such as the use of justice reinvestment programs, community-based programs, Circle Sentencing, the Youth Koori Court and the Walama List sentencing procedure, intended to reduce recidivism and examine the reasons behind offending.

Post-sentencing

The teacher may begin by exploring how this stage attempts to balance the interests of society and individuals through a range of initiatives. Primarily, students examine the use of imprisonment to protect society, but they should also investigate reforms in response to issues such as breaches of conditions and lack of resources.

Making connections

Teachers could make connections to the content from the Criminal law content group in the Year 11 focus area Disputes under the law. As the rights of individuals such as suspects, the accused, offenders and victims are explored, explicit links to rights protected under international instruments can be drawn to support understanding of the Year 12 focus area International relations and human rights (core).

Teachers are encouraged to explore a range of issues through the legal themes that offer students insight into the operation of the law.

Key skills

  • Develop informed judgements using criteria supported by evidence.
  • Communicate in a variety of ways to demonstrate a critical understanding of justice.
  • Explain the relationship between the legal themes and the criminal justice system.

The use of evidence

In Legal Studies, students develop their understanding of the law through investigating and analysing a range of evidence from a variety of sources. Evidence can be used to demonstrate how the law operates, support or refute an interpretation of the law, or inform legal reasoning.

Teachers can support students to effectively use evidence by:

  • selecting legislation that highlights the powers of police and areas of reform, such as the amendments to bail legislation
  • referring to a range of media reports that feature the effectiveness of diversionary programs
  • using hypothetical scenarios to demonstrate factors considered when sentencing an offender
  • providing opportunities to work independently to synthesise and integrate a range of current sources of information available online
  • using multimodal sources such as videos, podcasts, infographics and visual summaries
  • providing questions to help interpret and evaluate sources
  • modeling source evaluation by explicitly teaching how to assess the reliability, bias and usefulness of a source.
